title: The Science of Taste and Flavour Perception
instructions: For questions 1-8, read the text below. Use the word given in capitals at the end of each line to form a word that fits in the gap in the same line.
passage:
What we commonly call taste is, according to food scientists, a largely (1)___ experience, built from signals the tongue can detect combined with smell, texture and even sound.

The tongue itself registers only a handful of basic qualities, yet our (2)___ of flavour feels far richer than this short list would suggest. Much of that richness comes from the nose: smell is so (3)___ to flavour that food tastes noticeably blander when a bad cold blocks the nasal passages.

Texture plays a surprisingly large role too: identical flavourings taste different depending on whether a food is (4)___ or soft, a fact marketers exploit (5)___ when designing snacks. Even sound factors in: researchers have found that crisps eaten to the sound of a louder crunch are consistently rated as fresher and more (6)___, regardless of any actual difference in the product.

Colour, meanwhile, can create powerful and sometimes (7)___ expectations: diners given a familiar drink dyed an unexpected colour often report that it tastes wrong, even when the (8)___ itself has not changed at all.

questions.explanation: The adjective 'deceptive' (= giving a false impression) fits 'a largely ___ experience', describing taste as not quite what it appears to be.
The noun 'perception' is needed as the subject of 'feels far richer', referring to how flavour is mentally processed.
The adjective 'essential' (= absolutely necessary) fits 'smell is so ___ to flavour', showing how central smell is to the overall experience.
The adjective 'crunchy' is needed to contrast with 'soft' in 'whether a food is ___ or soft'.
The adverb 'deliberately' modifies the verb 'exploit', showing the action is intentional rather than accidental.
The adjective 'appealing' (= attractive) fits alongside 'fresher' as a second quality the crisps are rated on.
The negative prefix 'un-' plus the adjective suffix '-able' gives 'unpredictable', fitting expectations that can go either way depending on the diner.
The noun 'composition' (= the way something is made up) fits after 'the', referring to the drink's actual ingredients as opposed to its colour.
